title: The Shepherd of Tekoa
subtitle: Amos 1
description: A shepherd from Tekoa carries eight oracles in one formula, and the ring of judgment closes nation by nation until it lands on Israel.
paragraphs: Amos was not a court prophet and not a guild prophet. He was a sheepherder from Tekoa, a town in the hill country of Judah, south of Jerusalem, and the words that open his book are careful to place him exactly: what he saw came to him “in the days when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel”, and the text adds a marker everyone in his generation could date without a calendar, “two years before the earthquake”. It is the same northern court the story has just come from. Jeroboam II's Israel was at its widest borders and its richest ease, the reign Jonah's prophecy had promised, and God sent this southern shepherd north into the middle of it with a message that began as a sound more than a sentence: “The LORD roars from Zion and raises His voice from Jerusalem; the pastures of the shepherds mourn, and the summit of Carmel withers.” A lion's roar, heard from Judah's capital, aimed at the north, and the first thing it withers is the shepherds' own pastures.

What Amos carried into Israel was a set of eight oracles built on a single frame, and the frame is the sermon. Each one opens with the same formula from the LORD: “For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they threshed Gilead with sledges of iron.” The count is a Hebrew way of saying the measure is full and overfull, three sins and a fourth on top, too many to let pass. The charges against the nations are war crimes, and they are specific. Damascus had threshed Gilead, Israel's own land east of the Jordan, as a farmer threshes grain, except with sledges of iron on people. Fire is promised on the house of Hazael, exile for Aram. Then Gaza of the Philistines: “they exiled a whole population, delivering them up to Edom”, a whole people sold away in a single transaction, and fire on Gaza's walls, the remnant of the Philistines to perish. Then Tyre, the great trading partner to the north, charged with the same slave dealing, sharpened by a broken agreement: “they delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom and broke a covenant of brotherhood”. Oracle by oracle the ring closes around Israel, and any Israelite listening would have heard these first ones gladly. They are judgments on Israel's enemies, pronounced by Israel's God, in Israel's hearing.

The ring keeps narrowing, and the charges keep getting closer to home. Edom is not a stranger nation but a brother, Esau's people, and the charge is a family's charge: “he pursued his brother with the sword and stifled all compassion”, an anger that never burned out, carried across generations. The Ammonites are charged with the worst single act in the list, stated in the text's own plain words: “they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead in order to enlarge their territory”, murder as a land policy. Moab's crime is stranger and colder, a king's bones dug up and desecrated: “he burned to lime the bones of Edom’s king”. Then the formula turns toward God's own people, and Judah comes first, the shepherd's own south: “they reject the Law of the LORD and fail to keep His statutes”, and the promised fire falls on Jerusalem itself. By the time the seventh oracle ends, the pattern has done its work. The audience has nodded along through six judgments on foreigners and one on the sister kingdom. The eighth opening is identical, and it is the point of the whole book: “For three transgressions of Israel, even four, I will not revoke My judgment”.

Israel's charges are not war crimes. They are courtroom and marketplace crimes, the sins of a prosperous peace, and they are quoted here at the length the text gives them because no summary carries their weight: “they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals”. “They trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the earth; they push the needy out of their way. A man and his father have relations with the same girl and so profane My holy name.” “They lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge. And in the house of their God, they drink wine obtained through fines.” Every item is a perversion of something given: the courts, where the righteous are sold a verdict at a time; the pledge laws, which existed to protect a poor man's cloak; worship itself, carried on in clothes seized from debtors, with wine bought by fines squeezed out of the weak. The nations were judged for what they did to Israel and to each other in war. Israel is judged for what it does to its own poor in peacetime, beside its own altars.

Against the charges God sets his own record, and the oracle turns into something like a prosecution's closing argument, gift answered by insult: “it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them”, the giants of the land cleared out like cedars felled and roots burned. “I brought you up from the land of Egypt and led you forty years in the wilderness”, that Israel might take possession of the Amorite's land. “I raised up prophets from your sons and Nazirites from your young men. Is this not true, O children of Israel?” And then the answer Israel gave, the whole indictment in one verse: “But you made the Nazirites drink wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy.” They broke the Nazirites' vows with wine and gagged the prophets God had raised from their own sons. So the sentence falls, and its shape is futility: “Escape will fail the swift, the strong will not prevail by his strength, and the mighty will not save his life.” Runner, strongman, archer, horseman, all of them covered, until the last line: “Even the bravest of mighty men will flee naked on that day”. The eightfold ring was never mainly about the neighbors. It was a shepherd from Tekoa walking the formula around the map until it closed on the people applauding it, and the book has only just begun: ahead, the God who roared from Zion addresses Israel directly, and the next word is an invitation to listen, “Hear this word”.

title: Hear This Word
subtitle: Amos 3
description: Election means exposure: the lion roars, Samaria's luxury is summoned before witnesses, and five disasters end on the same refrain.
paragraphs: The second movement of the book opens with the address the first movement was circling toward: “Hear this word that the LORD has spoken against you, O children of Israel, against the whole family that I brought up out of the land of Egypt”. And the first sentence of the indictment is not about Israel's sins but about Israel's privilege, stated as the very grounds of the punishment: “Only you have I known from all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities.” Election, in Amos, is not a shield. It is an exposure. The one nation God had known out of all the families of the earth is the one nation held to account for everything, because it alone had been given the standard it broke. Then the prophet argues his own commission out of the way things work in the world, in a chain of cause and effect any farmer could follow. “Can two walk together without agreeing where to go?” A lion does not roar over nothing; a bird does not drop into a snare with no bait; a trap does not spring empty; a trumpet in a city means trouble; and “If calamity comes to a city, has not the LORD caused it?” The chain lands on two sentences that stand back to back as the book's charter: “Surely the Lord GOD does nothing without revealing His plan to His servants the prophets.” “The lion has roared”, and then the question, “who will not fear?” “The Lord GOD has spoken”, and then the question, “who will not prophesy?” Amos is not volunteering. He is the last link in the chain: the roar happened, so the shepherd speaks.

Then God does something a courtroom would recognize: He calls witnesses, and the witnesses He calls are Israel's enemies. The citadels of Ashdod and Egypt are invited to assemble on Samaria's mountains and look at what Israel does to its own: “Assemble on the mountains of Samaria; see the great unrest in the city and the acts of oppression in her midst.” The verdict on what the foreigners would see is one of the saddest lines in the book, because it is about competence at goodness itself: “For they know not how to do right,” declares the LORD. “They store up violence and destruction in their citadels.” The palaces are storehouses, and what is stored is violence. The sentence follows: an enemy will surround the land and plunder the strongholds. And the rescue, when it comes, is described in Amos's own trade, a shepherd's arithmetic of loss: “As the shepherd snatches from the mouth of the lion two legs or a piece of an ear, so the Israelites dwelling in Samaria will be rescued having just the corner of a bed or the cushion of a couch”. Proof of the kill, not a flock saved. A corner of a bed. A couch cushion. The summons ends at the sanctuary and the great houses together: at Bethel, “the horns of the altar will be cut off, and they will fall to the ground”, and in the cities, “the houses of ivory will also perish, and the great houses will come to an end”.

Chapter four opens with the book's most famous insult, aimed at the wealthy women of the capital: “Hear this word, you cows of Bashan on Mount Samaria, you women who oppress the poor and crush the needy, who say to your husbands”, and then their whole theology in four words, “Bring us more to drink.” Bashan was pasture country east of the Jordan, famous for fat cattle, and the comparison is an insult and an indictment in one: well-fed, self-indulgent, and driving the oppression personally, demanding to be kept in drink. The LORD has sworn by His holiness against them: “the days are coming when you will be taken away with hooks, and your posterity with fishhooks”. Carried out like fish, through the breaches in broken walls, each one straight ahead, cast out. Then, without pausing, the voice turns to the whole nation's worship and the irony runs like acid: “Go to Bethel and transgress; rebel even more at Gilgal! Bring your sacrifices every morning, your tithes every three days.” Offer the leavened bread, proclaim the freewill offerings loudly, “For that is what you children of Israel love to do”. Religion enthusiastically performed at the rival shrines, generosity announced, devotion on display, and every word of the invitation means the opposite: this is what your worship has become, a love of the performance, and God counts the performance itself as the transgression.

What follows is the book's saddest refrain, five sent disasters counted off like a case history, each one ending on the same four-beat line. First famine: “I afflicted all your cities with cleanness of teeth and all your towns with lack of bread, yet you did not return to Me,” declares the LORD. Clean teeth because there was nothing to eat with them. Then drought, rain mocked by its own selectivity, one city watered and its neighbor withered, people staggering from city to city for water and going unsatisfied, “yet you did not return to Me”. Then blight and mildew on the growing gardens: “I struck you with blight and mildew”, the locust took the fig and olive trees, “yet you did not return to Me”. Then plague and war, plagues like Egypt's, young men killed with the sword, the stench of the camp in their nostrils, “yet you did not return to Me”. Last, overthrow itself: “you were like a firebrand snatched from a blaze, yet you did not return to Me”. Some of them had been pulled out of burning like a stick out of a fire, Sodom's own escape, and even that did not turn them. The refrain is the point: every disaster had an address and a purpose, and the purpose failed, five times, in writing.

So the episode closes where the case history was always heading, on a meeting. “prepare to meet your God, O Israel!” Not prepare to meet an army, or a famine, or a conqueror. The disasters were couriers; the sender is coming Himself. And the God Israel is summoned to meet is then named in the book's first doxology, quoted whole because nothing shorter carries it: “He who forms the mountains, who creates the wind and reveals His thoughts to man, who turns the dawn to darkness and strides on the heights of the earth”, “the LORD, the God of Hosts, is His name”. The former of mountains and the maker of wind, the God who turns morning into darkness by walking the heights, has announced a meeting with a nation of altar-side pledge-seizers and bowl-drinking ease, and the shepherd from Tekoa is the one carrying the summons.

title: Seek Me and Live
subtitle: Amos 5
description: A funeral lament sung to a living nation, the open door of Seek Me and live, and justice rolling on like a river.
paragraphs: Chapter five opens with something a prophet does only when the verdict is already written: Amos sings Israel's funeral lament while Israel is still alive to hear it. “Hear this word, O house of Israel, this lamentation I take up against you”, and the song itself is three lines long: “Fallen is Virgin Israel, never to rise again. She lies abandoned on her land, with no one to raise her up.” The nation in the song is a young woman dead in a field with no one to lift her, and the tense is past, a death reported, not predicted. The arithmetic of it follows: “The city that marches out a thousand strong will have but a hundred left”, a ninety percent loss stated as calmly as a census. That the lament is sung in advance is itself part of the mercy of the book: a nation hearing its own funeral dirge still has ears, and ears are what the next words are aimed at.

Because immediately after the dirge, the alternative is offered, and offered as a refrain. “Seek Me and live!” The command is then spelled out by negation, because Israel's whole religious map ran the other way: “Do not seek Bethel or go to Gilgal; do not journey to Beersheba, for Gilgal will surely go into exile, and Bethel will come to nothing.” The shrines were the seeking. Pilgrimage, sacrifice, and feast at the king's sanctuary felt like seeking God, and the prophet strips the equation bare: the places are under sentence themselves, and a man cannot seek shelter in a condemned building. “Seek the LORD and live, or He will sweep like fire through the house of Joseph”, fire with no one at Bethel to put it out. Between the commands stands the book's second doxology, because the God who must be sought is not the god of the shrines: “There are those who turn justice into wormwood and cast righteousness to the ground.” “He who made the Pleiades and Orion, who turns darkness into dawn and darkens day into night, who summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth”, “the LORD is His name”, “He flashes destruction on the strong, so that fury comes upon the stronghold.” The maker of constellations and tides is the one being turned into wormwood justice by men who imagined Him housed.

The middle of the chapter names the mechanism, and it is the city gate, where Israel's courts sat and where the poor man's case went to die: “There are those who hate the one who reproves in the gate and despise him who speaks with integrity.” “For I know that your transgressions are many and your sins are numerous. You oppress the righteous by taking bribes; you deprive the poor of justice in the gate.” The consequence is measured out in the currency of the builders: because you trample the poor and tax his grain, “you will never live in the stone houses you have built; you will never drink the wine from the lush vineyards you have planted”. And the honest men have already learned the system's lesson: “the prudent keep silent in such times, for the days are evil”. Through it all the offer stands unrescinded, the refrain again in a new key: “Seek good, not evil, so that you may live. And the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be with you, as you have claimed.” “Hate evil and love good; establish justice in the gate. Perhaps the LORD, the God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Joseph.” Perhaps. The book of Amos does not deal in guaranteed outcomes; it deals in a door still open, with judgment on the threshold and grace stated as a possibility no one in the gate had earned.

Then the chapter turns on the nation's proudest expectation. Israel longed for the Day of the LORD, the day God would finally settle accounts with Israel's enemies, and Amos asks the book's most dangerous question: “Woe to you who long for the Day of the LORD! What will the Day of the LORD be for you? It will be darkness and not light.” The picture of it is a man escaping one death into the next: “It will be like a man who flees from a lion, only to encounter a bear, or who enters his house and rests his hand against the wall, only to be bitten by a snake.” Lion outside, bear behind, snake inside the house itself; there is no room in the sequence that is safe. And before the picture, the feasts come under the book's plainest rejection: “I hate, I despise your feasts! I cannot stand the stench of your solemn assemblies.” Offerings unaccepted, fattened cattle unregarded, and then worship's music itself dismissed: “Take away from Me the noise of your songs! I will not listen to the music of your harps.” In place of all of it, one sentence, the most quoted line Amos ever carried: “But let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.” Not a seasonal wadi that runs after rain and dries by summer, but a stream that never stops. God reaches back past the shrines to the wilderness to ask whether the sacrifices were ever the point: “Did you bring Me sacrifices and offerings forty years in the wilderness, O house of Israel?” What Israel had actually carried through those years, He says, were Sakkuth their king and Kaiwan their star god, idols of their own making, and so the sentence closes the chapter: “I will send you into exile beyond Damascus”, farther than the enemy capital the book began by judging.

Chapter six moves the camera from the gate to the couch. “Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria”, the distinguished men of the foremost nation, so secure they “dismiss the day of calamity and bring near a reign of violence”. The portrait is drawn from the furniture out: “You lie on beds inlaid with ivory, and lounge upon your couches. You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall.” They improvise songs on the harp like David, inventing instruments, anointing themselves with the finest oils, “You drink wine by the bowlful”, not by the cup. And in the center of the inventory, the one thing missing is named in a single line that carries the whole chapter: “you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph”. Joseph, the tribes, their own house, was ruining, and the men on the ivory beds had oil for their skin and wine by the bowl and not one unit of grief. The sentence matches the portrait: “you will now go into exile as the first of the captives, and your feasting and lounging will come to an end”, first in the column they refused to imagine. God swears by Himself against the pride of it: “I abhor Jacob’s pride and detest his citadels, so I will deliver up the city and everything in it.” What remains afterward is described in a whisper: in a house of ten, all die; the relative burning bodies asks if anyone is left inside, and the answer comes back with a warning attached, “Silence”, “for the name of the LORD must not be invoked”. Even prayer is hushed, for fear of what invoking the name might draw down. The book ends the movement with God's own rhetorical questions to a people who had inverted the world: “Do horses gallop on the cliffs? Does one plow the sea with oxen? But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood”. And against their boasting over two captured border towns, the last word is a nation raised from Lebo-hamath to the Brook of the Arabah, the whole length of the land Amos was sent to warn.

title: The Plumb Line and the Priest
subtitle: Amos 7
description: Amos argues God out of two visions, the plumb line ends the arguing, and at Bethel the king's priest meets the shepherd's only credential.
paragraphs: The last movement of the book changes its instrument. Up to now Amos has carried sermons; now the LORD shows him pictures, and the pictures are verdicts he is meant to watch being drawn. The first vision is locusts, prepared just after the king's harvest, as the late crop was coming up, the crop the people themselves depended on, and when the swarm had eaten every green plant in the land in the vision, the prophet does the one thing no earlier chapter showed him doing. He argues. “Lord GOD, please forgive! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?” And the book states the result as simply as the vision: “So the LORD relented from this plan.” “It will not happen,” He said. A second vision follows, judgment by fire, a fire that consumed the great deep and devoured the land, and Amos argues again with the same words, urgency sharpened: “Lord GOD, please stop! How will Jacob survive, since he is so small?” “So the LORD relented from this plan.” “It will not happen either,” said the Lord GOD. The man sent to pronounce the end of Israel twice talked God out of the end of Israel, on the grounds of the nation's smallness. It is the only intercession of its kind in the book, and it works twice. Then comes the third picture, and no argument follows it.

The third vision is a tool from Amos's own world, a builder's instrument: the Lord standing by a wall true to plumb, a plumb line in His hand, the weighted cord a mason hangs to test whether a wall stands straight or leans toward falling. “Amos, what do you see?” asked the LORD. Amos answered that he saw a plumb line. “Behold,” said the Lord, “I am setting a plumb line among My people Israel; I will no longer spare them”. The wall had been measured, and a wall out of plumb is not repaired in Amos's message; it is condemned. Intercession has a limit in this book, and the limit is not Amos's willingness, which is never withdrawn. It is the measurement. The sentence that follows names the whole structure: the high places deserted, the sanctuaries laid waste, and against the reigning house, “I will rise up against the house of Jeroboam with My sword”. It is at this point, and not before, that the institution answers back.

Amaziah, priest of Bethel, the king's sanctuary, reports the sermon to Jeroboam as treason: “Amos has conspired against you in the midst of the house of Israel. The land cannot bear all his words”. Then the priest turns on the prophet and delivers the establishment's whole case in three sentences: “Go away, you seer! Flee to the land of Judah; earn your bread there and do your prophesying there.” “But never prophesy at Bethel again, because it is the sanctuary of the king and the temple of the kingdom.” Amos is treated as a professional who has taken his trade to the wrong market: prophesy for bread if you must, but not here, not at the king's chapel. The answer Amos gives is the only autobiography in the book, and the series has waited four episodes for it: “I was not a prophet,” Amos replied, “nor was I the son of a prophet; rather, I was a herdsman and a tender of sycamore-fig trees.” No guild, no training, no father's office, no bread earned by prophesying. “But the LORD took me from following the flock and said to me”, and the command he quotes is the book's whole origin in one line: “Go, prophesy to My people Israel.” Amaziah had said do not preach against the house of Isaac; the word of the LORD answers the priest personally, and the answer is the harshest oracle in the book aimed at one man: “Your wife will become a prostitute in the city, and your sons and daughters will fall by the sword.” His land measured out and divided, himself dead on pagan soil, and the refrain under it all unchanged: “And Israel will surely go into exile, away from their homeland.” The confrontation at Bethel is the book's one prose scene, and it is a hearing: the king's priest cross-examines the shepherd, and the shepherd's only credential is that he was taken.

The fourth vision is the quietest and the worst: a basket of summer fruit, the harvest's end in a container. “Amos, what do you see?” He asked. The answer is the fruit. “The end has come for My people Israel; I will no longer spare them.” In the Hebrew the word for summer fruit and the word for end sound nearly the same, a pun no harvest could outrun: the fruit is ripe, and ripeness is the verdict. “the songs of the temple will turn to wailing. Many will be the corpses, strewn in silence everywhere!” The chapter then turns from the vision to the men the whole book has been watching, and lets them indict themselves out of their own mouths at their own counters: “When will the New Moon be over, that we may sell grain? When will the Sabbath end, that we may market wheat?” Religion was to them an interruption of business, and the business was rigged: “Let us reduce the ephah and increase the shekel; let us cheat with dishonest scales.” “Let us buy the poor with silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, selling even the chaff with the wheat!” Short measures, inflated prices, crooked scales, sweepings sold as grain, and human beings bought for the price of footwear, the same charge from the book's second chapter, now heard in the merchants' own voices. The oath that answers it is the chapter's coldest line: “The LORD has sworn by the Pride of Jacob: “I will never forget any of their deeds.”

The episode closes with the strangest sentence in the book, a judgment described as a famine that is not one. The sun forced down at noon, feasts turned to mourning, every head shaved, “like a time of mourning for an only son”, and then: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the Lord GOD, when I will send a famine on the land”, and the definition splits the sentence open: “not a famine of bread or a thirst for water, but a famine of hearing the words of the LORD”. “People will stagger from sea to sea and roam from north to east, seeking the word of the LORD, but they will not find it.” The nation that commanded its prophets not to prophesy will one day hunt the whole land for a word from God and find silence. It is the Bethel scene inverted and enlarged: they told the shepherd to take his words back to Judah, and the last famine of the book is a country searching for the voice it sent away. The young women and young men faint from a thirst no water answers, and those who swore by the guilt of Samaria and the god of Dan fall, in the chapter's final phrase, “never to rise again”, the same words the funeral lament used of Virgin Israel, now spoken of the worshipers who made her what she was.

title: No Escape, and the Booth of David
subtitle: Amos 9
description: The Lord stands by the altar and there is nowhere to hide; then the book turns: the fallen tent of David raised and a people planted for good.
paragraphs: The last vision of the book is not shown to Amos at a distance. “I saw the Lord standing beside the altar”, and the first words of the vision are a demolition order spoken from inside the sanctuary itself: “Strike the tops of the pillars so that the thresholds shake. Topple them on the heads of all the people, and I will kill the rest with the sword. None of those who flee will get away; none of the fugitives will escape.” Every earlier vision had a frame around it, locusts in a field, a fire, a plumb line, a basket. This one is a building coming down on the worshipers, commanded by the God they had come to worship, and the theme the whole vision sounds is the theme the episode is named for: there is nowhere left to run. The book that began with a roar from Zion ends its visions in the one place Israel believed was safest, and the altar gives no cover.

What follows is the most relentless pursuit passage in the prophets, and it is quoted at its own length because its accumulation is its meaning: “Though they dig down to Sheol, from there My hand will take them; and though they climb up to heaven, from there I will pull them down.” “Though they hide themselves atop Carmel, there I will track them and seize them; and though they hide from Me at the bottom of the sea, there I will command the serpent to bite them.” Down into the grave, up into the sky, to the summit of the green mountain, to the floor of the sea, even into captivity itself, where the sword is commanded to find them there too. It closes on a sentence that reverses one of Scripture's warmest assurances and means to: “I will fix My eyes upon them for harm and not for good.” The watching of God, which Israel sang about as protection, is here announced as pursuit. No prophet in the run has yet spoken of judgment with nowhere outside it; Jonah ran to the sea and found God already there, but he found Him appointing a fish, not a serpent.

Then, in the middle of the pursuit, the book stops for its third and last doxology, as if to say who it is that cannot be escaped: “He who touches the earth and it melts, and all its dwellers mourn”, the land rising and sinking like the Nile under His hand. “He builds His upper rooms in the heavens and founds His vault upon the earth. He summons the waters of the sea and pours them over the face of the earth. The LORD is His name.” And it is this God who then asks Israel the question that quietly removes the book's last remaining shelter, the assumption that the exodus made Israel untouchable: “Are you not like the Cushites to Me, O children of Israel?” declares the LORD. “Did I not bring Israel up from the land of Egypt, the Philistines from Caphtor, and the Arameans from Kir?” Other nations have exoduses too. Philistines and Arameans, Israel's oldest enemies, were also brought up and settled by the same hand, and election was never a fence. Yet inside the same breath the sentence carries its own limit, stated as an oath: “Yet I will not utterly destroy the house of Jacob,” declares the LORD. The sifting image that follows explains the difference: “I will shake the house of Israel among all the nations as grain is sifted in a sieve; but not a pebble will reach the ground.” Shaken among the nations like grain in a sieve, everything loose falling through, and not one solid kernel lost. The sinners who said disaster would never draw near die by the sword in the same oracle. The sieve is not mercy for everyone; it is precision, a judgment that can tell grain from rubble.

Then the book turns, and the turn is total. The last oracle of Amos begins with a day and a ruin: “In that day I will restore the fallen tent of David. I will repair its gaps, restore its ruins, and rebuild it as in the days of old”. David's house, divided since Rehoboam and fallen to a tent, a booth, a shepherd's shelter in this book's own vocabulary, is to be raised and mended, so that the restored people possess the remnant of Edom and all the nations that bear God's name. The harvest that follows is described in impossibilities: “the plowman will overtake the reaper and the treader of grapes, the sower of seed. The mountains will drip with sweet wine, with which all the hills will flow.” The crops come faster than they can be gathered, the sowing catches up with the harvest, abundance measured as a calendar collapsing. And the people of the sentence: “they will rebuild and inhabit the ruined cities. They will plant vineyards and drink their wine; they will make gardens and eat their fruit.” Every clause of it answers the book's own curses. In chapter five they were told they would never live in the houses they built or drink from the vineyards they planted; here they rebuild and inhabit, plant and drink, garden and eat. The exile beyond Damascus is reversed, not merely ended.

The book of Amos ends on a planting. The same voice that roared from Zion in the first verse, that summoned Israel to prepare to meet its God, that swore it would never forget a single deed, speaks the final sentence of the book, and the final sentence is a promise about roots: “I will firmly plant them in their own land, never again to be uprooted from the land that I have given them,” says the LORD your God. Planted is the last image, and uprooted is the last threat, and the threat is the one denied. No answer from Israel is recorded. The book closes the way it opened, on God's voice carrying the whole weight, but the voice that began by withering the summit of Carmel ends by planting a people in their own soil for good, and the shepherd who carried the word goes unnamed in its final lines, his work done, the word outliving the messenger exactly as he said it would.
